title: The Frame You Take With You
scopeNote: This keeps the performed task whole, because there is no way to preserve it except by performing it: judgements alone, then with three others, then alone again. The phases are shorter, the round-by-round comparison against three full simulated groups is reduced to their endpoints, and the explicit compliance contrast is moved into the synthesis.
summary: Eight trials watching a point of light drift in a dark field, judged on a 1 to 10 scale: three alone, three with three simulated others generated from your own opening judgements, and two alone again once they have gone. Whatever you do, the chart is yours and neither outcome is the right one.
learningObjectives: Say why a frame formed with others persists once they are gone.
Distinguish that from going along with a demand, which ends when the audience does.
Explain why ambiguity is what makes a group's figure stick.
Recognise that different groups settle on different values from the same rule.
Say why a norm is better described as what has stopped being a question than as what people have agreed.
interactionTypes: a performed judgement task in three phases
an animated ambiguous stimulus with a visible start and end to every trial
simulated others generated from the learner's own opening judgements
group information present only while the group is present
a chart of all four series revealed once the task is over
an honest report of the learner's own result, whichever way it went
privacy: Nothing is collected, stored or transmitted. What the learner chooses is used only to draw the chart in front of them and is discarded when the page is left. Nothing measures anything about the reader.
dataStatus: The three other participants are generated by a rule printed on the page. Nothing here reproduces the stimuli, procedure or data of any historical study.
stimulusNotes: The display is a browser analogue of Sherif's ambiguous movement judgement, not a replication of it, and the page says so in the opening note and again in the debrief. Sherif used the autokinetic effect, in which a stationary pinpoint of light in a darkened room appears to drift; that illusion needs darkness, dark-adapted eyes and a controlled viewing distance, so a web page cannot rely on it, and a display that only might move for some readers leaves them estimating something they never experienced. The point of light here therefore moves for real: three sine components per axis with seeded phases and frequencies between roughly 0.5 and 3 rad/s, so the path wanders rather than oscillating countably or jittering. Peak excursion is 38 to 78 viewBox units, different on every trial and never disclosed, against a point about 10 pixels across; measured in Chromium that is 111 to 134 pixels of path over five seconds at all three test widths. The field carries no ruler, grid, axis or reference object, and the trial ends with the field empty, so there is nothing left to measure against afterwards either. The stimulus keeps a set height and crops its width rather than scaling, so the rendered size of the point and of its displacement stays within a narrow band from 1440px to 320px. A reduced-motion preference halves the excursion and slows it rather than removing it, because a still point would recreate exactly the defect this display exists to avoid.
accessibilityNotes: Nothing is timed except the five-second trial itself, which the learner starts and which ends on its own. Every state of the display is reported in text beneath it: ready, running, and finished with the field empty. The figure's description says what the point of light does and that the field carries no scale of any kind. The response is a native range input with min 1, max 10 and step 1, with its anchors stated in the label and hint and its current value echoed as text; the recording function rounds and clamps whatever it is handed, so no value outside the scale can reach the model. Controls that are not yet available are marked aria-disabled rather than disabled, and the start button's own text says why. A learner who cannot see the field cannot perform the perceptual part, and the page does not pretend otherwise; the judgement is genuinely unconstrained for everyone, so the social mechanism still runs. The chart labels each series at the end of its own line and its description lists every judgement made. The group trials are shaded and also named in words.
simulationNotes: The three others are generated after the learner's opening judgements. Their centre sits 2.6 scale points from the learner's opening mean, on whichever side keeps it inside the 1 to 10 scale, with the three of them spread -1.3, 0.0 and 1.4 around it; on each later group trial each of them moves 45 per cent of the way towards the previous trial's four-person average, with a little noise, rounded and clamped. The gap is deliberate and is printed on the page with the rest of the rule: seeding the others directly on the learner's own mean puts the group's figure where the learner already is, which leaves nothing to converge towards and no way to read the result. Nothing about the learner is modelled or forced, so a learner who holds firm pulls the group rather than being overridden. Group information is present only while the group is: the panel appears after a group trial and is cleared once the judgement is in, the record table drops the others' columns entirely for the final solo trials, and the chart showing their lines is not drawn until the task is over. The ending handles three cases honestly. A learner who ends nearer the group is told the pattern matched and, in as many words, what it is not: their figures had gone, nobody would see the last two answers, and there was no cost to answering as at the start. A learner who does not move is told it is not a failure and not a sign of anything about them, and that a single run of eight trials could not distinguish holding a frame from reading the display consistently all along. There is always a real comparison to report: sweeping the shipped model over every non-decreasing opening triple and four group strategies, 880 runs, the learner's opening average and the figure the other three finish on are never closer than 1.0 scale points, which is what the 2.6-point gap is for and what the test suite asserts. Three further simulated groups are shown as openings and endpoints only, because the between-group point, that the value a group settles on is arbitrary, needs nothing else.
readmeTopic: why a figure worked out with other people is still there when they have gone
